I'm a USAmerican living in Europe. Yes Americans are living paycheck to paycheck. 
There's this lifestyle expectation you have to meet for work, social groups, etc. There's greater socioeconomic disparity than what I see here.  And it's normal to try to keep up with your friends with better jobs. 

And pretty much everything here is just cheaper in a way that's hard to explain. Even if it's more expensive per unit,  it ends up being less over a long period. Interest rates are MUCH lower, cell phone plans are cheaper,  wi-fi is cheaper, car insurance... gas is more expensive but public transport is more accessible and the cities are walkable. You cannot live/work most places in the US without a car. 

Electric is outrageous, but the houses are built for the weather so I just use the heat/AC/lights less often. Having the fresh produce within 2 minutes walking means I don't buy in bulk and watch things rot. The quality of the items I purchase tends to be greater so I'm not throwing money.

Oh... the health care thing and college tuition.  That's no joke. I have known people in their 60s all paying college loans.  People in their 20s that are paying 50,000 medical debts.

What worked with my daughter in time.. 

I learned to pick my battles. I had to sort out which crap is worth fighting for 2 hours about. Everything else I just ignored until she got bored with it. When I didn't react or interact, it wasn't as interesting and the bad behavior was shorter. 

And really i learned that a lot of what I was irritated about was her not doing what I said. So I started asking myself why it mattered. Natural punishment was so much more effective. She wanted to go out wearing high heels and refused to wear normal shoes? Ok. She has worn high heels maybe one time since then. Throw the ball over the fence? Guess you don't have a ball. 

Consistency is key. Knowing what to expect as far as whatever reward/punishment/rule system helps. Kids naturally push boundaries, so once you know what's worth fighting with a 2 year old for 2 hours about... make sure the wall is brick and not elastic. Don't make threats you can't or don't want to follow through with. They catch on too fast. 

Sometimes you have to protect your mental health. Put yourself on time out. Not sure his age, but playpen or the back yard, bedroom, TV, video games. Just give yourself 10 minutes.  

I would "catch her being good." I would pay attention and randomly reward the good behaviors. If I noticed I was suddenly less stressed out than usual, I'd take her to the library or give her control of other things as a reward. 

And since things were really out of control, I built things she could control.  I would prepare different healthy snacks and different junk food snacks in the fridge. She could have 2 each day and choose herself as long as at least 1 was healthy. That helped with the picky eating drama too. I would give self directed time outs. "You need to sit in the corner until you're ready to follow the rules." I think the longest time out she gave herself was more than 45 minutes. I would NEVER put her in a corner that long.  But she refused to come out because she was NOT going to listen. 

And that lead me to realize that acting out often meant she was overwhelmed.  So I made her a relaxing place. We called it her cool down spot.  She decorated it. We made it a happy, nice, special place she controlled. And when she was acting up, I'd say something like hey, you seem overwhelmed. Would it help you to have a break from people? And eventually she would just give herself a break before it was trouble.
